analysis.one_liner: Requires many employers without retirement plans to automatically enroll workers in payroll-deduction IRAs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2015 and referred to two House committees, but never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require employers with more than 10 employees who offer no retirement plan to automatically enroll workers in an IRA funded through payroll deductions, with the workers free to opt out or withdraw. Employers would face a $100-per-employee penalty for failing to provide the arrangement, and small employers would get a tax credit to help with setup. Workers without a workplace plan — roughly half of private-sector workers at the time — would gain a simple way to save for retirement.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees at firms with more than 10 workers that offer no retirement plan: they would be automatically enrolled in an IRA funded by payroll deductions (default 3% of pay), protected by an opt-out, and free to withdraw. Small employers (100 or fewer employees) would receive a tax credit to offset setup costs. Because savings accumulate through payroll, workers who never had a workplace retirement account gain one by default.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with no retirement plan at work

how_it_helps.text: Covered employers must make an automatic IRA available to every qualifying employee, with a default contribution of 3% of pay (adjustable between 2% and 6%), unless the employee opts out or terminates participation. [S2][S3]
Employers who fail to provide the arrangement face a $100 penalty per employee for each year of failure, with waivers for reasonable-cause failures and a 90-day correction window. [S3]

Employers with 100 or fewer employees receive a tax credit of $25 per participating employee (capped at 10 employees) plus $500 in the first year and $250 in the second to offset administrative costs. [S2][S3]

The bill directs the Treasury Secretary to provide a model notice and website so small employers can easily find notices, forms, and lists of retirement plan providers, reducing the administrative burden that often deters small firms from offering plans. [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Employers without retirement plans bear administrative costs for payroll deposits, notices, and remitting contributions on schedule; those who fail to comply owe $100 per affected employee per year. The Treasury (federal taxpayers) bears the revenue cost of the new small-employer tax credits and the existing IRA deduction that the new automatic contributions would claim. Financial firms offering the IRAs would face limits on charging unreasonable extra fees for small accounts.

drawbacks.text: Employers without plans face new compliance work (notices, payroll remittances) and a $100-per-employee penalty for failures, a real cost for small and low-margin businesses even with the startup credit. [S3]

Automatic enrollment defaults workers into contributing 3% of pay unless they act, which could reduce the take-home pay of lower-income workers who would not have chosen to save — though they can opt out or withdraw within 90 days without penalty. [S3]
The bill adds federal tax subsidies (the small-employer credit and expansion of the existing startup-credit limit), increasing federal costs and adding complexity to the tax code. [S2][S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — giving workers without a workplace plan a default way to save — is substantial and cheap for taxpayers compared with the small-employer credits the bill adds. The main costs fall on a narrow group: employers with more than 10 employees who currently offer nothing, who would face modest administrative work and penalties for noncompliance. The default-contribution design, standard in behavioral retirement policy, protects workers through opt-out rights and an early withdrawal window, so the risk to unwilling savers is limited but real for workers living paycheck to paycheck.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Ways and Means and Education and the Workforce committees without ever getting a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and the 114th Congress ended with it still stuck in committee.

narrative.text: Rep. Richard Neal (D-MA) introduced the Automatic IRA Act of 2015 on January 22, 2015. [S1][S5]
The bill was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and, additionally, to the House Education and the Workforce Committee. [S5]

In April 2015 the Education and Workforce Committee referred it to its Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions; in October 2015 the Ways and Means Committee referred it to its Subcommittee on Health. [S5]
No further action occurred for the remainder of the 114th Congress: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate companion is recorded in the bill's action history. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers without workplace retirement plans are worse off because the bill never advanced, leaving them without the automatic savings mechanism it would have provided. Employers without plans are better off, having avoided new compliance obligations and potential penalties.

industries.industry: Employers without retirement plans (retail, food service, small firms)
industries.note: They would have to set up payroll deductions, issue notices, and remit employee savings on schedule, or owe $100 per affected employee per year. This is the group the requirement is aimed at.

industries.industry: Financial firms offering IRAs and investment products
industries.note: The bill creates a new stream of small payroll-deduction accounts funneling savings to IRA providers and mutual funds, with an advisory group of providers helping set the rules. The bill does restrict 'unreasonable additional fees' on small accounts, but the industry gains millions of new customers by default.

The bill directs the Treasury Secretary to issue a new 'retirement bond' as a default low-cost option for first-time savers, expanding the government's role as a savings provider — though the bill's stated intent is that long-term savings eventually move to the private market.
